Reproducing Chen, He et al. (2026) from dandiset 001933¶

Paper: Chen C, He Q, Tombesi G, et al. (2026). Leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 impairs the release sites of Parkinson's disease vulnerable dopamine axons. Nature Communications. doi:10.1038/s41467-026-75194-3. This attempt used the open access full text (CC BY) and its Supplementary Information.

Dandiset: DANDI:001933, version 0.260825.1457. This version was asked for: it is the version of the earlier attempt, chen-2026-01, and the dandiset has not changed since (the data check shows the version and the draft hold the same files). It is also the only published version, and the paper names neither the dandiset nor a version (its data statement points to Zenodo, PRIDE and the BioImage Archive).

This is attempt chen-2026-02, under protocol pilot-7. The data are the same as in attempt -01; the protocol changed. Pilot-7 adds a kind of claim, data: elsewhere, for a claim whose data the paper deposited in another public archive. The eight claims of Figures 1 to 5, blocked in attempt -01 as data_missing, are such claims: they now name their archive and are tested here on those data, counted apart from the dandiset's claims. The ten photometry claims and their criteria are unchanged and are re-run. The data check also says, for each finding of attempt -01, whether it still holds.

What the dandiset holds: one session per mouse of GRAB-DA3m fiber photometry in the dorsal striatum during optogenetic stimulation of SNc dopamine neurons, 15 Anxa1-iCre mice (dorsolateral striatum) and 12 Calb1-Cre mice (dorsomedial striatum), LRRK2-WT and LRRK2-G2019S (GS). This is the data of Figure 6 and Supplementary Figures 7 and 8.

Outside data: the paper's Zenodo record (10.5281/zenodo.19930567): the source data file, used in source-data-link and as the per-section, per-area and per-blot values of Figures 1, 2, 4 and 5, and the Supplementary data files; PRIDE PXD065006 (phosphopeptide abundances) and PXD065125 (pulldown intensities and the DIA-NN report); and the BioImage Archive, where the synaptosome images of S-BIAD2074 are streamed and measured and the file lists of S-BIAD2070, 2071 and 2072 are matched to the source data. The paper's photometry code was read at DombeckLab/lrrk2_photometry_analysis, commit d34558f, and its proteomics R code in the Zenodo record (analysis code.zip). The Imaris analyses of Figures 1 and 5 and the Proteome Discoverer search of Figure 2 use commercial software and are not re-run.

fig5j-no-axon-loss No loss of TH+ fibres elsewhere: S-BIAD2072, Zenodo tested

Method choices are fixed in the claims file, claims/001933/10.1038-s41467-026-75194-3.yaml. In short: the signal is the dandiset's processed dF/F, the trace the paper's code analyses; the evoked integral follows the Methods (the light-on period), with the code's baseline; spontaneous transients follow the Methods and transient_by_threshold.m. The claims of Figures 1 to 5 use the legends' tests on the deposited values, and for Figure 4D and 4E also the Methods' FIJI procedure, re-implemented in archives.py, on the images.

Data check¶

Each check of the description against the values is stated under its output. The check covers the dandiset, the findings of attempt -01, and the data of Figures 1 to 5 in other archives.

The files hold one session each of 15 Anxa1 mice (8 GS, 7 WT) and 12 Calb1 mice (7 GS, 5 WT), the paper's counts after its exclusions, and the Anxa1 GS mouse IDs are those of the Figure 6E legend. The four excluded mice are not in the dandiset, which does not say that they were left out. Ages at the session are 6.3 to 7.6 months, consistent with surgery at 6 months and recording four weeks later. Anxa1 mice are recorded in the dorsolateral and Calb1 mice in the dorsomedial striatum, as the paper states. No two files share a dF/F trace or a start time, so no recording is deposited twice. The pinned version and the draft hold the same files.

rows = []
for s in sessions:
    t, x = s["t"], s["dff"]
    dt = np.diff(t) * 1000
    rows.append({"mouse": s["mouse"], "line": s["line"], "group": s["group"], "samples": len(t),
                 "first_s": round(t[0], 2), "minutes": round((t[-1] - t[0]) / 60, 1),
                 "dt_med_ms": round(np.median(dt), 2), "dt_min_ms": round(dt.min(), 2), "dt_max_ms": round(dt.max(), 2),
                 "dff_min": round(x.min(), 1), "dff_p8": round(np.percentile(x, 8), 2), "dff_max": round(x.max(), 1),
                 "dff405_min": round(s["dff405"].min(), 1), "dff405_max": round(s["dff405"].max(), 1),
                 "max_diff_recomputed": round(np.abs(x - s["dff_recomputed"]).max(), 4),

The processed series are regular at 10 ms (the shortest interval, 9.5 ms, comes from the 2 kHz grid) and last 20.4 to 25.4 min, a little longer than the Methods' 20 min. The dF/F series is stated in a.u., but its description and its values are % dF/F: the code's df_f and 20-sample moving mean applied to the stored corrected signal give the stored series to within 0.026 % dF/F. The raw 470 nm signal, averaged into the 100 Hz bins, aligns with the corrected signal at lag 0 in every file (correlation 0.77 to 0.99), so raw and processed series share a clock. About 8 of the 20 raw samples per bin are kept for 470 nm, as the demultiplexing describes.

for s in sessions:
    p = s["power_in_mW"]
    dur = s["stop_time"] - s["start_time"]
    paper = np.isin(p, lrrk2.PAPER_POWERS)
    gaps = np.diff(s["start_time"])
    rows.append({"mouse": s["mouse"], "line": s["line"], "group": s["group"], "epochs": len(p),
                 "per_power": "/".join(str((p == q).sum()) for q in sorted(set(p))),
                 "powers": len(set(p)), "first_8_codes": "".join(code_letter[q] for q in p[:8]),
                 "paper_powers_in_half": 1 if paper[:32].all() else (2 if paper[32:].all() else 0),
                 "train_s_paper": round(np.median(dur[paper]), 3), "pulse_ms_paper": s["pulse_length_in_ms"][paper][0],
                 "period_ms_paper": s["period_in_ms"][paper][0],
                 "train_s_other": round(np.median(dur[~paper]), 3), "pulse_ms_other": s["pulse_length_in_ms"][~paper][0],
                 "period_ms_other": s["period_in_ms"][~paper][0],
                 "min_gap_s": round(gaps.min(), 1), "median_gap_s": round(np.median(gaps), 1),

Every file holds 64 trains, 8 at each of 8 powers from 0.1 to 4 mW; the paper uses four of them (0.1, 0.5, 1 and 4 mW). The table's own description gives 8 ms on and 8 ms off for 500 ms and only those four powers, but the table holds two kinds of train. In Anxa1 files one half of the session has 9 ms pulses every 10 ms for 0.33 s, the other 8 ms pulses every 16 ms for 0.51 s; Calb1 files hold only the second kind. The paper's four powers fall on 0.51 s trains in 25 files and on 0.33 s trains in two Anxa1 GS mice (3742 and 4885), so these two mice were stimulated differently from every WT mouse; a variant of fig6e-anxa1-evoked-reduced leaves them out. One train each in mice 4652 and 740 has a pulse length of 0, no period and one pulse, though it lasts 0.51 s like its neighbours, so its pulse columns are wrong. Trains of the same power come in pairs 15.3 to 15.5 s apart, and 51% of the gaps are under 20 s, where the Methods and the table description say at least 20 s.

rows = []
for s in sessions:
    shifted = dict(s, onset=s["onset"] + 1000, offset=s["offset"] + 1000)  # 10 s later, between trains
    true = lrrk2.evoked_integrals(s, "fixed")
    moved = lrrk2.evoked_integrals(shifted, "fixed")
    iso = lrrk2.evoked_integrals(s, "fixed", trace="dff405")
    traces = np.array([s["dff"][i - 100:i + 300] for i in s["onset"] if i + 300 <= len(s["dff"])])
    mean_trace = traces.mean(0)
    ok = ~np.isnan(true)
    rows.append({"mouse": s["mouse"], "line": s["line"], "group": s["group"],
                 "median_at_onsets": np.nanmedian(true), "median_10s_later": np.nanmedian(moved),
                 "median_405_at_onsets": np.nanmedian(iso),
                 "peak_latency_ms": (np.argmax(mean_trace) - 100) * 10,
                 "rise_before_onset": mean_trace[90:100].mean() - mean_trace[:90].mean(),
                 "spearman_power": stats.spearmanr(s["power_in_mW"][ok], true[ok])[0],
                 **{f"{q}mW": np.nanmedian(true[s["power_in_mW"] == q]) for q in sorted(set(s["power_in_mW"]))}})
clock = pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values(["line", "group", "mouse"])
print("Integral from 0 to 0.5 s after onset minus the mean of -1.0 to -0.1 s (% dF/F x s), median over each file's 64",
      "trains, at the table's onsets, 10 s later, and for the 405 nm control; latency of the peak of the mean trace;",
      "Spearman correlation of the integral with the labelled power; median integral per labelled power.")
print(clock.round(2).to_string(index=False))
print("\nFiles where the median at onsets exceeds the median 10 s later:", int((clock.median_at_onsets > clock.median_10s_later).sum()),
      "of", len(clock), "; Wilcoxon p =", f"{stats.wilcoxon(clock.median_at_onsets, clock.median_10s_later).pvalue:.2g}")
print("Peak latency (ms) from", clock.peak_latency_ms.min(), "to", clock.peak_latency_ms.max(),
      "; mean rise in the 0.1 s before onset from", clock.rise_before_onset.min().round(2), "to", clock.rise_before_onset.max().round(2))
print("Spearman correlation with power, median by line:", clock.groupby("line").spearman_power.median().round(2).to_dict())

# The two Anxa1 G2019S mice whose paper powers are 0.33 s trains, against two GS mice given 0.51 s trains,
# one epoch per row: labelled power, train type and the 0 to 0.5 s integral.
rows = []
for m in (3742, 4885, 4004, 4651):
    s = by_mouse[m]
    v = lrrk2.evoked_integrals(s, "fixed")
    for j in range(len(v)):
        rows.append({"mouse": m, "epoch": j, "power": s["power_in_mW"][j],
                     "train_s": round(s["stop_time"][j] - s["start_time"][j], 2),
                     "train": "0.33 s, 9/10 ms" if s["period_in_ms"][j] == 10 else "0.51 s, 8/16 ms", "pulse_ms": s["pulse_length_in_ms"][j],
                     "period_ms": s["period_in_ms"][j], "integral_0_0.5s": v[j]})
ep = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print("\nEpoch by epoch, mice 3742 and 4885 (0.33 s trains at the paper's powers) and 4004 and 4651 (0.51 s trains):")
for m in (3742, 4885):
    print(ep[ep.mouse == m].round(2).to_string(index=False))
print("\nMedian 0 to 0.5 s integral by labelled power and train type:")
print(ep.pivot_table(index=["mouse", "train"], columns="power", values="integral_0_0.5s", aggfunc="median").round(1).to_string())
print("Spearman correlation of the integral with labelled power, within each train type:")
print(ep.groupby(["mouse", "train"]).apply(lambda g: round(stats.spearmanr(g.power, g["integral_0_0.5s"], nan_policy="omit")[0], 2)).to_string())

# Anxa1 files where 1.5, 2 and 3 mW are 0.33 s trains and 0.5 and 1 mW are 0.51 s trains: do the former fall below?
rows = []
for s in sessions:
    if s["line"] != "Anxa1":
        continue
    v = lrrk2.evoked_integrals(s, "fixed")
    kind = {q: set(s["period_in_ms"][s["power_in_mW"] == q]) for q in (0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0)}
    if not (all(kind[q] == {10} for q in (1.5, 2.0, 3.0)) and all(kind[q] == {16} for q in (0.5, 1.0))):
        continue
    med = {q: np.nanmedian(v[s["power_in_mW"] == q]) for q in kind}
    rows.append({"mouse": s["mouse"], "group": s["group"], **{f"{q}mW": med[q] for q in kind},
                 "high_033_below_low_051": max(med[q] for q in (1.5, 2.0, 3.0)) < min(med[q] for q in (0.5, 1.0))})
split = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print("\nAnxa1 files with 1.5, 2 and 3 mW as 0.33 s trains and 0.5 and 1 mW as 0.51 s trains, median 0 to 0.5 s integral:")
print(split.round(1).to_string(index=False))
print("Files where every 0.33 s median (1.5, 2, 3 mW) is below both 0.51 s medians (0.5, 1 mW):",
      int(split.high_033_below_low_051.sum()), "of", len(split))

Files where every 0.33 s median (1.5, 2, 3 mW) is below both 0.51 s medians (0.5, 1 mW): 7 of 12

At the table's onsets the 0 to 0.5 s integral has a median of 13 to 260 % dF/F x s per file; 10 s later, between trains, it is near zero in every file (lower in 27 of 27, Wilcoxon p = 1.5e-08), and the 405 nm control shows no response (medians -0.74 to 1.15). The mean response peaks 160 to 370 ms after onset. The mean trace rises by up to 25 % dF/F in the 0.1 s before onset: the 20-sample moving mean of the stored dF/F spreads the response about 0.1 s earlier, which is why the code's baseline ends 0.1 s before onset. The epochs table and the photometry share a clock.

The response grows with the labelled power in every Calb1 file (Spearman 0.76 to 0.94) but not in many Anxa1 files (median 0.06). Of the 12 Anxa1 files where 1.5, 2 and 3 mW are given as 0.33 s trains and 0.5 and 1 mW as 0.51 s trains, the 0.33 s responses fall below both 0.51 s ones in 7 (for example mouse 4401) and not in the other 5 (in 4398, 173.5 at 1.5 mW against 114.8 at 0.5 mW). The power labels are consistent with the data in Calb1 files; in Anxa1 files the data alone cannot confirm them. The labels of the four powers the paper uses are confirmed against its source data under source-data-link.

The epoch-by-epoch tables show mice 3742 and 4885, whose paper powers are all 0.33 s trains of 9 ms pulses every 10 ms, and two GS mice given 0.51 s trains. In 3742 the response does not follow the labelled power: within the 0.33 s trains the median 0 to 0.5 s integral is lowest at 0.5 mW (5.7 % dF/F x s) and higher at 0.1 mW (33.5), and the correlation with power is negative within each train type. In 4885 the 0.33 s trains give medians of 35.0 to 53.5 at the four labelled powers, below every 0.51 s power (56.1 to 78.1), and the correlation with power is negative within both train types (-0.28 and -0.74). In 4004 and 4651 the response rises with power within the 0.51 s trains (Spearman 0.81 and 0.86) and not within the 0.33 s ones (-0.41 and -0.21). The data cannot confirm the power labels of 3742 and 4885.

Findings of attempt chen-2026-01¶

The same version is analysed again, so each finding of the earlier attempt is checked against the files, the archive's metadata, the paper's code repository and the paper's Crossref record.

The data in other archives¶

The claims of Figures 1 to 5 are tested on the data the paper deposited elsewhere (protocol pilot-7, data: elsewhere): the tabular values behind each figure on Zenodo, the search outputs in PRIDE and the images in the BioImage Archive. Each is read in memory. This check lists what each archive holds, counts it against the legends, and looks for values or files deposited twice.

The source data file read here is the one in the Zenodo record (equal md5). Its counts agree with the legends for Figures 1D (16 sections, 3 mice), 2E and 2G (10 and 7 per group), 4D (39 WT and 35 GS areas), 4G to 4L (6 mice per genotype), 5D, 5G, 5H and 5J. They disagree in two places: Figure 4E has 51 GS areas where the legend gives 57, and Figure 5E has 21 GS Aldh1a1+ sections where the legend gives 20. One GS value of Figure 4D, 0.0766 %, is of the size of the Figure 4E areas (0.04 to 0.15) and may have been pasted from there; it is kept, and leaving it out is shown. Sections 4 and 5 of WT mouse 1723 in Figure 5D and 5E carry the same four values to six digits, so one section appears to have been entered twice; as the claims file fixes, it is counted once, and the values as deposited are a variant. Figure 5D holds a density of 0 for one WT Aldh1a1- section, kept as deposited. The other repeated values (one in 4D, one in 5E) are single values, not whole sections. The sheets of Figure 5G/5H and 5J give one animal column for both genotypes, holding WT IDs (1021, 1024, 1028; 3244, 3757, 3874, 4434), so the GS animals of these panels are not identified in the source data. The values carry no units; Figure 1D and 5J are normalised to about 1.

The peptide groups table of PXD065006 equals the PeptideGroups sheet of Supplementary data 1: 8008 phosphopeptides with three vehicle and three MLi-2 samples, of which 5366 have all six values and 6070 at least two per group. It holds the RAB3 peptide YRTITTAYYR phosphorylated at T86 of RAB3A and RAB3B (T92 of RAB3C). The paper's volcano table, also in Supplementary data 1, holds 6157 peptides. The pulldown matrix of PXD065125 holds 3480 protein groups, the paper's count. Its twelve pulldown columns equal runs C13 to C24 of the DIA-NN report, and the SDRF gives p-RAB3A for C13 to C18 and RAB3A for C19 to C24, so the column labels agree with the runs. The pairing of replicates behind the paired test of Figure 3E and 3F is not stated; run order is used, as the claims file fixes.

import re


def ids(paths, pattern):
    out = []
    for p in paths:
        m = re.search(pattern, p.split("/")[-1])
        out.append(m.groups() if m else (None, None))
    return out

The images match the source data by mouse only in part, and none of the studies records which images the figures used. S-BIAD2070 holds 7 images for each of the three Figure 1D mice, where the source data give 5 or 6 sections each. S-BIAD2071 holds Aldh1a1 images of the four GS mice of Figure 5D (1272, 1522, 517, 796) and of WT mice 1923, 1929, 516 and 797, where the source data name 1723 for the first; two WT files carry no mouse ID. Its Anxa1 folder holds four WT mice (1018, 1021, 1024, 1028), where the legend and the source data have three (1018 is not in the source data), and four GS mice (1019, 1020, 1022, 1052) that the source data do not name. In S-BIAD2072, the volume folder holds 16 images for each of the four WT mice of Figure 5J and of four GS mice (3243, 3246, 4120, 4369), 64 per genotype, where the legend gives 8 images per section for 12 sections (96). S-BIAD2074 names its images by genotype and a mouse number from 1 to 5. Its counts do not follow the source data image by image: in the BSN folder the GS mice have 14, 10 and 12 images against 14, 11 and 10 areas in Figure 4D (WT 14, 10, 15 against 14, 11, 14); in the BSN-area folder GS has 50 images against 51 areas (and the legend's 57) and WT 43 against 43 (cell 75 drops one GS image with no particle to measure). Part B of fig4d-fewer-active-zones therefore compares genotypes over the deposited images and cannot match them to the published areas.

All 168 synaptosome images were streamed and measured, and no two share content, although the BSN and BSN-area folders share file names for mice 1 and 3. One image (ki4 BSN1) is 512 x 512 at 0.0615 um per pixel, the others 1024 x 1024 at 0.0308 or 0.0311 um; particle sizes use each image's own pixel size. With the Methods' procedure as re-implemented here, an image holds 1 to 417 VAMP2 particles (median 183), well under the legend's "about 1000 synaptosomes per area", and one image in each folder has nothing to measure. The re-implementation does not reproduce the paper's segmentation closely (it is not FIJI, and the threshold and perimeter are approximations), and part B of the claim is read with that in mind.

The OME metadata of 165 images give excitation at 488, 561 and 640 nm for channels 0, 1 and 2, the order the archive annotates (bassoon, TH, VAMP2). Three images of GS mouse 4 in the BSN-area folder (BSN2, BSN3 and BSN4) give 488 nm for all three channels; they are read in the same order as the others. Before the size and circularity limits, the Default threshold gives a median of 1186 VAMP2 objects per image, near the legend's "about 1000"; the size limit of 0.04 to 0.40 um2 alone leaves 193, and the circularity limit 183. The figure shows that the kept particles are the brighter puncta and that many dimmer puncta fall below the threshold. Which step differs from the paper's FIJI run cannot be told from these outputs.

Claims¶

source-data-link¶

The dandiset's recordings are those behind the paper's Figure 6 and Supplementary Figures 7 and 8, and the paper's published per-stimulation traces, evoked integrals and spontaneous transient integrals can be recomputed from them.

Records are matched by mouse ID, group, labelled power and the rank of the stimulation within its power. The source data file is read in memory from Zenodo.

In [11]:
md5, src = lrrk2.load_source_data()
print("Source data file md5:", md5, "; matches the Zenodo record:", md5 == lrrk2.SOURCE_DATA_MD5)
print("Records per table:", {k: len(v) for k, v in src.items()})
line_of = {"6C": "Anxa1", "6E": "Anxa1", "6F": "Anxa1", "S7B": "Anxa1", "S7C": "Anxa1",
           "S8C": "Calb1", "S8D": "Calb1", "S8E": "Calb1"}

# (1) Mice
mice = {(k, d["mouse"], d["group"]) for k, v in src.items() for d in v}
part1 = pd.DataFrame([{"table": k, "mouse": m, "group": g, "in_dandiset": m in by_mouse,
                       "same_group": m in by_mouse and by_mouse[m]["group"] == g,
                       "same_line": m in by_mouse and by_mouse[m]["line"] == line_of[k]} for k, m, g in mice])
part1["match"] = part1.in_dandiset & part1.same_group & part1.same_line
mouse_level = part1.groupby("mouse").match.all()
print(f"\n(1) Mice: {int(mouse_level.sum())} of {len(mouse_level)} source-data mice are in the dandiset with the same genotype and line;",
      "dandiset mice not in the source data:", sorted(set(by_mouse) - set(mouse_level.index)))


def rank_match(records):
    """Pair each source record with the dandiset epoch of the same mouse and power and the same rank."""
    seen, out = {}, []
    for d in records:
        key = (d["mouse"], d["power"])
        r = seen.get(key, 0)
        seen[key] = r + 1
        s = by_mouse[d["mouse"]]
        idx = np.where(np.isclose(s["power_in_mW"], d["power"]))[0]
        out.append((d, s, idx[r], idx))
    return out


# (2) Triggered traces
rows = []
for key in ("6C", "S7B", "S8D"):
    for d, s, j, idx in rank_match(src[key]):
        ours = lrrk2.code_chunk(s, j)
        rows.append({"table": key, "line": s["line"], "mouse": d["mouse"], "power": d["power"],
                     "max_diff": np.nanmax(np.abs(ours - d["trace"])), "nan_here": int(np.isnan(ours).sum()),
                     "r": np.corrcoef(ours[~np.isnan(ours)], d["trace"][~np.isnan(ours)])[0, 1],
                     "slope": np.polyfit(ours[~np.isnan(ours)], d["trace"][~np.isnan(ours)], 1)[0],
                     "offset": np.polyfit(ours[~np.isnan(ours)], d["trace"][~np.isnan(ours)], 1)[1]})
part2 = pd.DataFrame(rows)
part2["match"] = part2.max_diff < 1e-6
print("\n(2) Triggered traces equal to the dandiset's dF/F from 1 s before the onset of the epoch with the same power and rank:")
print(part2.groupby("table").agg(records=("match", "size"), matched=("match", "sum"), largest_diff=("max_diff", "max"),
                                 median_r=("r", "median"), slope_min=("slope", "min"), slope_max=("slope", "max")).to_string())
print("Largest difference among matched traces, per table:", {k: f"{v:.2g}" for k, v in part2[part2.match].groupby("table").max_diff.max().items()})
print("Unmatched Anxa1 traces:")
print(part2[(part2.line == "Anxa1") & ~part2.match].to_string(index=False))
m4398 = by_mouse[4398]
print(f"Mouse 4398: last onset at {m4398['start_time'][-1]:.2f} s, processed series ends at {m4398['t'][-1]:.2f} s")

# (3) Evoked integrals
code_auc = {s["mouse"]: lrrk2.evoked_integrals(s, "code") * lrrk2.FS for s in sessions}  # in samples, as the code
rows = []
for key in ("6E", "S7C", "S8E"):
    for d, s, j, idx in rank_match(src[key]):
        four = np.where(np.isclose(s["power_in_mW"], 4.0))[0][list(idx).index(j)]
        rows.append({"table": key, "line": s["line"], "mouse": d["mouse"], "power": d["power"], "published": d["value"],
                     "ours": code_auc[d["mouse"]][j], "ours_4mW_same_rank": code_auc[d["mouse"]][four]})
part3 = pd.DataFrame(rows)
factor = float(np.nanmedian(part3.published / part3.ours))
part3["match"] = np.abs(part3.published - factor * part3.ours) <= 1e-4 * np.abs(part3.published)
part3["match_if_4mW"] = np.abs(part3.published - factor * part3.ours_4mW_same_rank) <= 1e-4 * np.abs(part3.published)
print(f"\n(3) Evoked integrals: common factor published / ours (code's window, in samples) = {factor:.6g}")
print(part3.groupby(["table", "power"]).agg(records=("match", "size"), matched=("match", "sum"),
                                            matched_if_4mW=("match_if_4mW", "sum")).to_string())
print("Calb1 records: ratio published / ours from", part3[part3.line == "Calb1"].eval("published / ours").min().round(6),
      "to", part3[part3.line == "Calb1"].eval("published / ours").max().round(6))
print("Unmatched Anxa1 records:", part3[(part3.line == "Anxa1") & ~part3.match][["table", "mouse", "power", "published", "ours"]].to_dict("records"))

# (4) Spontaneous transients
measures = {ex: {s["mouse"]: lrrk2.spontaneous_transients(s, ex) for s in sessions} for ex in ("methods", "code_as_written")}
rows = []
for key in ("6F", "S8C"):
    pub = pd.DataFrame(src[key])
    for m, g in pub.groupby("mouse", sort=False):
        row = {"table": key, "line": line_of[key], "mouse": m, "published": len(g)}
        for ex in ("methods", "code_as_written"):
            auc, peaks, means, per_duration = measures[ex][m]
            row[f"n_{ex}"] = len(auc)
            for name, v in (("integral", auc), ("mean", means), ("per_duration", per_duration)):
                ratio = g.value.values / v if len(v) == len(g) else np.array([np.nan])
                row[f"{name}_ratio_{ex}"] = np.median(ratio)
                row[f"{name}_ratio_cv_{ex}"] = np.std(ratio) / np.mean(ratio)
        rows.append(row)
part4 = pd.DataFrame(rows)
for ex in ("methods", "code_as_written"):
    for name in ("integral", "mean", "per_duration"):
        f4 = np.nanmedian(part4[f"{name}_ratio_{ex}"])
        for rtol, tag in ((1e-2, ""), (1e-4, "_1e-4")):
            ok = []
            for _, r in part4.iterrows():
                pub = pd.DataFrame(src[r.table]).query("mouse == @r.mouse").value.values
                v = measures[ex][r.mouse][{"integral": 0, "mean": 2, "per_duration": 3}[name]]
                ok.append(len(pub) == len(v) and bool(np.allclose(np.sort(pub), f4 * np.sort(v), rtol=rtol, atol=0)))
            part4[f"match_{name}_{ex}{tag}"] = ok
            print(f"(4) exclusion '{ex}', {name} of each transient: common factor {f4:.6g}; mice whose count and sorted values match",
                  f"within a relative {rtol:g}:", int(np.sum(ok)), "of", len(ok), "(Anxa1", int(np.sum(np.array(ok)[part4.line == 'Anxa1'])), "of 15)")
cols = ["table", "mouse", "published", "n_methods", "n_code_as_written", "integral_ratio_cv_methods", "mean_ratio_methods",
        "mean_ratio_cv_methods", "match_integral_methods", "match_mean_methods", "match_mean_methods_1e-4",
        "match_mean_code_as_written"]
print(part4[cols].to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.4g}"))
for _, r in part4[(part4.line == "Anxa1") & ~part4.match_mean_methods].iterrows():
    pub = np.sort(pd.DataFrame(src[r.table]).query("mouse == @r.mouse").value.values)
    v = np.sort(measures["methods"][r.mouse][2]) * float(np.nanmedian(part4.mean_ratio_methods))
    rel = np.abs(pub - v) / np.abs(pub)
    print(f"Anxa1 mouse {r.mouse} fails the 1% match on the mean: {int((rel > 1e-2).sum())} of {len(rel)} sorted values differ by more",
          f"than 1% (largest {rel.max():.3g}); its own ratio {r.mean_ratio_methods:.6g}, CV {r.mean_ratio_cv_methods:.3g}")
print("Transients: published", part4.published.sum(), "; here, Methods exclusion", part4.n_methods.sum(),
      "; code's exclusion as written", part4.n_code_as_written.sum())
print("Count equal to the published count, Methods exclusion:", part4.groupby("line").apply(lambda g: f"{int((g.published == g.n_methods).sum())} of {len(g)}").to_dict())

score = {"mice": float(mouse_level.mean()), "traces": float(part2.match.mean()), "evoked integrals": float(part3.match.mean()),
         "spontaneous integrals (best window)": float(max(part4.match_integral_methods.mean(), part4.match_integral_code_as_written.mean()))}
print("Part (4) with integrals at a relative 1e-4, the tolerance of part (3):",
      round(float(max(part4["match_integral_methods_1e-4"].mean(), part4["match_integral_code_as_written_1e-4"].mean())), 3))
print("\nFraction of records that match, per part, as the criterion scores them:", {k: round(v, 3) for k, v in score.items()})
print("Variant, part (4) with the mean dF/F of each transient, within 1%:",
      round(float(max(part4.match_mean_methods.mean(), part4.match_mean_code_as_written.mean())), 3), "; within 1e-4:",
      round(float(max(part4["match_mean_methods_1e-4"].mean(), part4["match_mean_code_as_written_1e-4"].mean())), 3))

# (4b) Which measure the published values are: for each candidate, the spread of published / ours within each mouse
# (transients in time order, Methods exclusion), and the mice that match at a relative 1e-4.
rows = []
for name in ("integral", "mean", "per_duration"):
    for line, g in part4.groupby("line"):
        rows.append({"measure": name, "line": line, "common_factor": float(np.nanmedian(part4[f"{name}_ratio_methods"])),
                     "largest_within_mouse_cv": float(g[f"{name}_ratio_cv_methods"].max()),
                     "median_within_mouse_cv": float(g[f"{name}_ratio_cv_methods"].median()),
                     "mice_matched_1e-4": f"{int(g[f'match_{name}_methods_1e-4'].sum())} of {len(g)}",
                     "mice_matched_1%": f"{int(g[f'match_{name}_methods'].sum())} of {len(g)}"})
print("\n(4b) Candidate measures of the published spontaneous values (per_duration: the trapezoid integral divided by the",
      "number of samples in the transient, % dF/F):")
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.6g}"))
score_pd = dict(score, **{"spontaneous integrals (best window)": float(max(part4["match_per_duration_methods_1e-4"].mean(),
                                                                          part4["match_per_duration_code_as_written_1e-4"].mean()))})
print("Variant, part (4) with the integral divided by the number of samples, at 1e-4; the four parts:", {k: round(v, 3) for k, v in score_pd.items()})

# (6) The paper's statistics recomputed from its own published values, to check the source data against the text.
pubdf = {k: pd.DataFrame(src[k]) for k in ("6E", "6F", "S7C", "S8C", "S8E")}
rows = []
for key, power, paper_p in (("6E", 0.5, "1.10e-20"), ("S7C", 4.0, "2.39e-16"), ("S8E", 0.5, "0.0002"), ("S8E", 4.0, "0.001")):
    g = pubdf[key][pubdf[key].power == power]
    gs, wt = g[g.group == "GS"].value, g[g.group == "WT"].value
    rows.append({"panel": key, "power": power, "n_GS": len(gs), "n_WT": len(wt), "p_one_tailed": lrrk2.one_tailed_less(gs, wt)[1],
                 "paper_p": paper_p, "cohens_d": lrrk2.cohens_d(wt, gs)})
for key, paper_p in (("6F", "2.75e-177"), ("S8C", "0.98")):
    g = pubdf[key]
    gs, wt = g[g.group == "GS"].value, g[g.group == "WT"].value
    rows.append({"panel": key, "power": np.nan, "n_GS": len(gs), "n_WT": len(wt), "p_one_tailed": lrrk2.one_tailed_less(gs, wt)[1],
                 "paper_p": paper_p, "cohens_d": lrrk2.cohens_d(wt, gs)})
print("\n(6) Statistics from the published values themselves (paper's Cohen's d at 0.5 mW: Anxa1 2.05, Calb1 0.76):")
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.3g}"))

To see why the Calb1 records differ, the dF/F is recomputed from the raw 470 nm signal in the dandiset with the code's binning and baseline correction, at the code's background fraction (0.85 of the sliding 8th percentile) and at other fractions, and compared with the published triggered traces. The edges of the sliding percentile are not reproduced exactly, so the comparison with the stored series leaves out the first and last 30 s.

# (5) Why the Calb1 records differ: dF/F recomputed from the raw 470 nm signal in the dandiset with the code's
# processing, and with other background fractions, against the published triggered traces.
rows = []
for s in sessions:
    binned = lrrk2.raw_binned(s)
    key = "6C" if s["line"] == "Anxa1" else "S8D"
    pairs = [(d, j) for d, ss, j, idx in rank_match([d for d in src[key] if d["mouse"] == s["mouse"]])]
    stored_diff = np.abs(lrrk2.dff_from_raw(binned) - s["dff"])[3000:-3000].max()
    best = None
    for frac in np.round(np.arange(0.0, 0.951, 0.05), 2):
        dff = lrrk2.dff_from_raw(binned, frac)
        err = np.median([np.abs(dff[s["onset"][j] - 100:s["onset"][j] + 150] - d["trace"]).max() for d, j in pairs])
        if frac == 0.85:
            at_085 = err
        if best is None or err < best[1]:
            best = (frac, err)
    rows.append({"mouse": s["mouse"], "line": s["line"], "group": s["group"], "stored_vs_recomputed_max_diff": stored_diff,
                 "median_diff_at_0.85": at_085, "best_fraction": best[0], "median_diff_at_best": best[1]})
raw_check = pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values(["line", "group", "mouse"])
print("Largest difference between the stored dF/F and dF/F recomputed from raw with the code's 0.85 (away from the edges),",
      "and the median over a mouse's published traces of the largest difference to dF/F recomputed with background fraction",
      "0.85 and with the best fraction of 0 to 0.95 (% dF/F):")
print(raw_check.round(3).to_string(index=False))

rows = []
for d, s, j, idx in rank_match(src["S8D"]):
    chunks = np.array([lrrk2.code_chunk(s, k) for k in range(len(s["onset"]))])
    ok = ~np.isnan(chunks).any(1)

    r = np.array([np.corrcoef(c, d["trace"])[0, 1] if o else -np.inf for c, o in zip(chunks, ok)])
    kd, kr = int(np.argmin(diff)), int(np.argmax(r))

Result: not reproduced. All 27 mice in the source data are in the dandiset with the same genotype and line. For Anxa1 the link holds: 120 of 120 triggered traces of Figure 6C and 479 of 480 of Supplementary Figure 7B equal the dandiset's dF/F from 1 s before onset (largest difference among matched traces 5.7e-13 in each table), the published evoked integrals equal the code's measure times 0.0001 for all Anxa1 records except one (119 of 120 at 4 mW), and the transient counts match for 15 of 15 mice. The two Anxa1 misses are the last 4 mW stimulation of mouse 4398, whose processed series ends 0.8 s after onset. For Calb1 none of the 384 traces and none of the 384 integrals match, and the transient counts match for 1 of 12 mice. dF/F recomputed from the raw signal with the code's processing reproduces the stored Calb1 series (largest difference 1.47 % dF/F) but not the published traces (median differences 66 to 519 % dF/F at the code's background fraction, and 22 to 88 at the best fraction for each mouse). The published spontaneous values are not integrals: they are 0.005 times the trapezoid integral divided by the number of samples in the transient (part 4b: within-mouse spread of the ratio at most 2.2e-15, 15 of 15 Anxa1 mice matched at 1e-4). Part (4) as the criterion fixed it, with integrals, matches for no mouse. Scored as the criterion sets out, the four parts match for 1.0, 0.609, 0.609 and 0 of their records, so the outcome is not reproduced. With the published measure in part (4) the parts give 1.0, 0.609, 0.609 and 0.556 (15 of 27 mice, no Calb1 mouse), which would be partially reproduced; the criterion fixed integrals, so this is a variant. The Figure 6E integrals match the 0.5 mW epochs (120 of 120) and none of the 4 mW ones, so the figure uses the power its legend states. The published values reproduce the paper's statistics (Figure 6E p = 1.1e-20, Figure 6F p = 2.75e-177, Supplementary Figure 8C p = 0.989, Cohen's d 2.06 and 0.765).

Part (4) scores 0 with integrals at either tolerance, 1% or the 1e-4 of part (3). The mean dF/F over each transient comes close (13 of 15 Anxa1 mice within 1%, none within 1e-4, per-mouse factor 0.004994 to 0.004999), as it differs from the published measure only in weighting the two end samples.

The Calb1 mismatch is not one of epoch or power labels. Against the matched epochs the published S8D traces have per-mouse median correlations of 0.76 to 0.99, median slopes of 0.21 to 0.75 and median offsets of -13.8 to 16.2 % dF/F. Searched over all 64 epochs and all 8 powers of each mouse, no epoch is within 1e-6 of any of the 384 traces; the closest differs by 15.7 to 150.8 % dF/F (median 47.1). Correlation does not single out an epoch: the epoch with the highest correlation is the matched one for 7 of 384 traces and has the labelled power for 86. The published Calb1 traces are smaller and differently shaped versions of the dandiset's responses, which points to processing; the dandiset does not hold that processing.

Evoked integrals¶

Integrals for every train under the four windows: the Methods' light-on period (main), the code's -0.1 to 1.0 s (code), the window chunking_index.m computes as written, starting 1 s after onset (code_as_written), and a fixed 0 to 0.5 s (fixed). All use the mean from 1.0 to 0.1 s before onset as baseline (shifted with the window for code_as_written).

In [14]:
def evoked_table(window):
    rows = []
    for s in sessions:
        values = lrrk2.evoked_integrals(s, window)
        for j, v in enumerate(values):
            rows.append({"mouse": s["mouse"], "line": s["line"], "group": s["group"], "power": s["power_in_mW"][j],
                         "train_s": round(s["stop_time"][j] - s["start_time"][j], 2), "value": v})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)


windows = ["methods", "code", "code_as_written", "fixed"]
evoked = {w: evoked_table(w) for w in windows}
print("Evoked integrals (% dF/F x s) that could not be computed (window outside the recording):",
      {w: int(evoked[w].value.isna().sum()) for w in windows})


def group_test(df):
    gs, wt = df[df.group == "GS"].value.dropna(), df[df.group == "WT"].value.dropna()
    t, p = lrrk2.one_tailed_less(gs, wt)
    return {"n_GS": len(gs), "n_WT": len(wt), "mean_GS": gs.mean(), "mean_WT": wt.mean(),
            "t": t, "p_one_tailed": p, "cohens_d": lrrk2.cohens_d(wt, gs)}


def per_mouse_tests(df, alpha):
    wt = df[df.group == "WT"].value.dropna()
    rows = []
    for m, g in df[df.group == "GS"].groupby("mouse"):
        v = g.value.dropna()
        row = {"mouse": m, "n": len(v), "mean": v.mean(), "WT_mean": wt.mean()}
        for name, equal_var, tails in (("a_welch_1t", False, 1), ("b_welch_2t", False, 2),
                                       ("c_student_2t", True, 2), ("d_student_1t", True, 1)):
            p = (lrrk2.one_tailed_less(v, wt, equal_var)[1] if tails == 1 else lrrk2.two_tailed(v, wt, equal_var)[1])
            row[f"p_{name}"] = p
            row[f"sig_{name}"] = bool(p < alpha and v.mean() < wt.mean())
        rows.append(row)
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

fig6e-anxa1-evoked-reduced¶

Optogenetically evoked dopamine release in the dorsolateral striatum (Anxa1+ projection region) at 0.5 mW is lower in LRRK2-G2019S than in LRRK2-WT mice (64 against 56 stimulations, p = 1.10e-20, one-tailed two-sample t-test).

The plot shows the mean dF/F (shading: SEM over stimulations) at 0.5 mW, with the 405 nm control dashed, and the light-on period shaded. All points are within the axes; the ranges are printed.

for w in windows:
    for q in (0.5, 4.0):
        r = group_test(evoked[w].query("line == 'Anxa1' and power == @q"))
        rows.append({"window": w, "power": q, **r})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.3g}"))

      f"{lrrk2.one_tailed_less(anxa[anxa.group == 'GS'].groupby('mouse').value.mean(), anxa[anxa.group == 'WT'].groupby('mouse').value.mean(), False)[1]:.3g}")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.8))
tt = np.arange(-100, 150) / lrrk2.FS
for ax, line in zip(axes, ("Anxa1", "Calb1")):
    for group, colour in (("GS", "tab:blue"), ("WT", "tab:gray")):
        tr, iso = [], []
        for s in sessions:
            if s["line"] != line or s["group"] != group:
                continue
            for j in np.where(s["power_in_mW"] == 0.5)[0]:
                tr.append(lrrk2.code_chunk(s, j))
                on = s["onset"][j]
                iso.append(s["dff405"][on - 100:on + 150])
        tr, iso = np.array(tr), np.array(iso)
        m, se = tr.mean(0), tr.std(0, ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(tr))
        ax.plot(tt, m, color=colour, label=f"{group} (n = {len(tr)})")
        ax.fill_between(tt, m - se, m + se, color=colour, alpha=0.3)
        ax.plot(tt, iso.mean(0), color=colour, ls="--", lw=1)
        print(f"{line} {group}: mean trace from {m.min():.1f} to {m.max():.1f} % dF/F; 405 nm mean from {iso.mean(0).min():.1f} to {iso.mean(0).max():.1f}")
    ax.axvspan(0, 0.5, color="red", alpha=0.1)
    ax.set_title(f"{line}, 0.5 mW (dashed: 405 nm)")
    ax.set_xlabel("time from onset (s)")
    ax.set_ylabel("dF/F (%)")
    ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Result: reproduced. At 0.5 mW there are 64 GS and 56 WT stimulations, as in the paper. The mean integral over the light-on period is 48.8 against 128.0 % dF/F x s, one-tailed p = 1.16e-22 (paper 1.10e-20), Cohen's d 2.21. With the code's window p = 1.1e-20, the paper's value. The reduction holds at 4 mW (p = 4.08e-18), without the two GS mice given 0.33 s trains (p = 4.16e-17), and with one value per mouse (Welch p = 0.000434). The window chunking_index.m computes as written reverses the sign (one-tailed p = 1, means -11.8 and -33), as it starts 1 s after onset. Every GS mouse except 3743 has a lower mean than every WT mouse (GS 3.28 to 82.33 without 3743, WT 90.86 to 190.21).

Result: reproduced. Under all four readings 7 of 8 GS mice are below the WT group at p < 0.05/8, and 3743 is the exception (mean 125 against 128, Welch one-tailed p = 0.362), as in the paper. The Student one-tailed p-values are of the same order as the legend's, for example 1.01e-04 against 4.0e-04 for 4651 and 3.73e-16 against 4.14e-15 for 3742. With the code's window the count is 7 under every reading, and at 4 mW it is 7 under the Welch readings. Two of the seven, 3742 and 4885, received their paper powers as 0.33 s trains, unlike every WT mouse, and the data cannot confirm their power labels (data check); the other five significant mice are 4004, 4005, 4007, 4651 and 4652.

Spontaneous transients¶

Transients for every mouse, with the Methods' exclusion of 1 s before to 1.5 s after each onset (main) and with the window the code removes as written (1 s to 3.5 s after onset). Each transient's integral, peak and mean dF/F are kept.

In [19]:
def spont_table(exclusion):
    rows = []
    for s in sessions:
        auc, peaks, means, per_duration = lrrk2.spontaneous_transients(s, exclusion)
        rows += [{"mouse": s["mouse"], "line": s["line"], "group": s["group"], "value": a, "peak": p, "mean": m, "per_duration": d}
                 for a, p, m, d in zip(auc, peaks, means, per_duration)]
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)


spont = {ex: spont_table(ex) for ex in ("methods", "code_as_written")}
for ex, df in spont.items():
    print(f"{ex}: {len(df)} transients over {df.mouse.nunique()} mice; integral (% dF/F x s) from {df.value.min():.2f} to {df.value.max():.1f}")

Result: partially reproduced. By the integral, the measure the criterion fixed, 5 of 8 GS mice are below the WT group under every reading. The exceptions are 3743 (Welch one-tailed p = 0.431), 4651, whose mean (417) is above the WT mean (303), and 4652 (p = 0.0128). With the published measure, 0.005 times the integral divided by the number of samples, reading (d), the one-tailed Student test of the legend, gives 6 of 8 with 3743 and 4651 as the exceptions, and the legend's p-values (3742 5.28e-88, 3743 0.965 against 0.97, 4004 1.24e-95, 4005 4.13e-109, 4007 5e-107, 4651 0.00844 against 0.008, 4652 6.21e-13, 4885 1.44e-49). The Welch readings give 7 there, as 4651 reaches p = 1.61e-05, so the paper's count follows the one-tailed Student test of its legend, not the Welch test of its Methods. The difference from the paper comes from the measure, not the data.

In the dorsomedial striatum (Calb1+ projection region), spontaneous dopamine transients are not reduced in G2019S mice (970 against 682 transients, p = 0.98).

Result: reproduced. By the paper's test, GS transients are not significantly smaller: one-tailed p = 0.0509 on 896 GS and 635 WT transients (both within tolerance of 970 and 682), difference of means 21.1 % dF/F x s, Cohen's d 0.085. The result sits at the threshold and is fragile: moving either end of the exclusion window by up to 10 samples gives p from 0.0403 to 0.0792, below 0.05 in 59 of 121 windows. With the published measure (0.005 times the integral divided by the number of samples) GS are lower at p = 2.45e-09 (d = 0.305), with the mean dF/F over each transient at p = 2.25e-09, and with the code's exclusion window as written at p = 1.81e-05; with one value per mouse, Welch p = 0.402. The dandiset's Calb1 dF/F is not the trace the paper analysed (see source-data-link), and the published values give p = 0.989.

Result: reproduced. There are 56 GS and 40 WT stimulations per power, as in the paper. GS are lower at all four powers, one-tailed p from 4.38e-07 (4 mW) to 6.29e-10 (0.5 mW), smaller p-values than the paper's 6.45e-05 to 0.001; the published integrals do not come from the dandiset's Calb1 dF/F (see source-data-link). With one value per mouse (7 GS and 5 WT), Welch one-tailed p is 0.0424, 0.0413, 0.0726 and 0.0916 at 0.1, 0.5, 1 and 4 mW, so the reduction is significant across mice at the two lower powers only.

cohens-d-anxa1-larger¶

The G2019S reduction of evoked release at 0.5 mW is much larger for Anxa1+ (Cohen's d = 2.05) than for Calb1+ stimulation (d = 0.76).

        dc = lrrk2.cohens_d(*[evoked[w].query("line == 'Calb1' and power == @q and group == @g").value.dropna() for g in ("WT", "GS")])
        rows.append({"window": w, "power": q, "d_Anxa1": da, "d_Calb1": dc, "ratio": da / dc})
cd = pd.DataFrame(rows)

Result: not reproduced. At 0.5 mW, Cohen's d is 2.21 for Anxa1, within tolerance of 2.05, and 1.40 for Calb1, against 0.76 (tolerance 0.684 to 0.836); their ratio is 1.58, below the factor of 2 the criterion asks. With the code's window d is 2.06 and 1.25. The published integrals give 2.06 and 0.765 (see source-data-link), so the paper's values follow from its own data, and the Calb1 difference is consistent with the Calb1 dF/F in the dandiset not being the one the paper analysed. The Anxa1 effect is larger than the Calb1 effect at every power under the Methods, code and fixed windows (ratio 1.29 to 1.74).

Claims on data in other archives¶

These eight claims rest on data that the dandiset does not hold and that the paper deposited elsewhere. They are data: elsewhere claims and are counted apart from the dandiset's. Each section names the archive.

Result: not reproduced. On the log2 abundances as deposited, 1694 (reading a) or 1810 (reading b) phosphopeptides pass p <= 0.05 and |difference| > 0.58, against the paper's 289, and nearly all are lower with vehicle (1673 and 1785), as the samples labelled MLi-2 have higher abundances overall (median log2 17.84 to 18.12, against 17.25 to 17.47). The RAB3 T86 peptide passes (p = 0.00892) but is lower with vehicle (difference -1.31), so neither part of the criterion holds. Centring each sample on its median, a step the criterion did not fix, gives 243 (a) and 282 (b) peptides, within tolerance for reading b, and RAB3 T86 is still higher with MLi-2 (difference -0.693, p = 0.0238). The paper's own volcano table holds MLi-2 minus vehicle as the samples are labelled: on the 4340 peptides with all six values its difference equals that difference plus a constant (-0.0043 after median-centring, -0.624 as deposited) to within 1.6e-06, while against vehicle minus MLi-2 the residual reaches 13. Its p-values are close to those of a t-test on the median-centred values but not equal (median gap in -log10 p 0.0088 for Welch, 0.0161 for Student), so its test or normalisation differs in a way that does not affect the difference. The table holds 254 peptides at the legend's thresholds and gives RAB3 T86 +0.688, which the legend reads as higher with vehicle. As the samples are labelled in PRIDE and in Supplementary data 1, the RAB3 T86 phosphopeptide is higher after MLi-2, the opposite of the claim, so either the labels or the direction of the figure is swapped. The canonical LRRK2 site RAB10 T73 does not change (0.15, p = 0.775), so the data cannot tell which. If the labels are swapped, the median-centred reading b gives 282 peptides and RAB3 T86 higher with vehicle (+0.693), which would reproduce the claim, so the outcome rests on a labelling question the data cannot answer.

unphos_cols = [f"unphos_{k}" for k in range(1, 7)]
rows = []
for gene in ("Rims1", "Rims2", "Rilpl1", "Rilpl2"):
    for _, r in pull[pull.Genes == gene].iterrows():
        rows.append({"gene": gene, "protein_group": r["Protein.Group"], "n_unphos": int(r[unphos_cols].notna().sum()),
                     "n_phos": int(r[phos_cols].notna().sum()), **archives.paired_test(r)})
res3 = pd.DataFrame(rows)
res3["values"] = res3.n_unphos + res3.n_phos
res3["used"] = False
for gene, g in res3.groupby("gene", sort=False):
    res3.loc[g["values"].idxmax(), "used"] = True
print("Paired two-sided t-test of log2 intensity, RAB3A against p-RAB3A pulldowns (paper: RIM2 p = 0.011, RILPL1 p = 0.002):")
print(res3.to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.3g}"))

holds = {g: bool((used.loc[g, "log2FC_unphos_minus_phos"] > 0) == g.startswith("Rims") and used.loc[g, "p"] < 0.05) for g in used.index}

      sum(holds.values()), "of 4")

# Variant: the same paired test on intensities without the log.

print("Variant, paired t-test on linear intensities (the first group of each gene):", {k: round(float(v), 4) for k, v in lin.items()})
r2 = pull[pull.Genes == "Rilpl2"].iloc[0]

      "; the paired test has no pair, so the criterion's test does not find RILPL2 higher with p-RAB3A")

Result: partially reproduced. In the PRIDE pulldown matrix, RIM1 (Q99NE5-7) and RIM2 are higher with RAB3A (log2 differences 2.42 and 2.17, paired p = 0.00361 and 0.0124) and RILPL1 is higher with p-RAB3A (-6.02, p = 9.8e-05). RILPL2 is detected in all six p-RAB3A pulldowns and in none of the RAB3A ones, so the criterion's paired test has no pair and does not find it higher with p-RAB3A: three of four comparisons hold. The data point the way of the claim for RILPL2: with the Methods' imputation, a variant, it is higher with p-RAB3A (log2 difference -7.92, p = 1.21e-08), and the deposited limma table gives logFC -7.58. The other two RIM1 groups agree (paired p = 0.0196 and 0.00984). The paper's p-values for RIM2 and RILPL1 (0.011 and 0.002) are those of the paired test on intensities without the log (0.0109 and 0.0022). The deposited limma table agrees in direction for every group. At the text's p-value < 0.05 and |log2FC| >= 1 it gives 121 and 32 proteins; the paper's 69 and 16 are the counts at adjusted p < 0.05.

Result: partially reproduced. (A) In the source data, fewer TH+/VAMP2+ synaptosomes contain bassoon in GS (12.0 against 21.4 %, p = 6.38e-05; 0.000118 without the value under 1 %) and the bassoon area is larger (0.0862 against 0.0750 um2, p = 0.0301, the paper's value), so part A holds. Both tests treat imaging areas as independent; with one value per mouse (3 or 4 per group) p = 0.263 and 0.474. (B) The Methods' FIJI procedure as re-implemented here finds neither effect in the images: 48.8 against 52.4 % with bassoon (GS against WT, p = 0.459), and a bassoon area of 0.0682 against 0.0696 um2 (overlap, p = 0.805) or 0.132 against 0.141 um2 (bassoon particle, p = 0.206). The re-implementation keeps far fewer synaptosomes than the paper (median 183 VAMP2 particles per image against about 1000; the threshold alone gives a median of 1186 objects, and the size limit removes most of them) and finds percentages more than twice the paper's. Part B may therefore fail because of this attempt's segmentation, and its null result is weak evidence against the claim.

Result: reproduced. RIM1 in synaptosomes is lower in GS (0.206 against 0.319, two-tailed p = 0.0245, the paper's value; Cohen's d -1.53), and RIM1 in the S1 fraction (p = 0.896) and in the SNc (p = 0.936) does not differ. Synaptophysin (4G, p = 0.445) and the protein of 4H (p = 0.634) do not differ either. The test starts from the deposited band values.

Result: partially reproduced. Five of the six parts hold. With section 5 of WT mouse 1723 counted once (its four values equal those of section 4), Aldh1a1+ density is lower in GS (0.164 against 0.217) but the Sidak-adjusted p is 0.058, so part 1 fails; Aldh1a1- density does not differ (p = 0.713). Bassoon volume is larger in GS Aldh1a1+ axons (Sidak p = 0.0425) and not in Aldh1a1- axons (p = 0.699). In Anxa1+ axons density is lower (p = 0.0374) and volume larger (p = 0.0148), the paper's values. With the section counted twice, as deposited, all six parts hold and the ANOVA gives the legend's numbers (5D: F 12.75, 1.277, 4.838, Sidak p 0.0344; 5E: Sidak p 0.0385). The legend's genotype F for 5E (1.277) repeats that of 5D; the deposited values give F = 5.234 with the legend's p = 0.0252. The analysis starts from the per-section values; the SIM images were not analysed again.

The photometry outcomes are those of attempt -01: the data, the code and the numbers are the same. After the first verification round, fig3d-rim-binds-unphosphorylated was changed from reproduced to partially reproduced, as its criterion's paired test cannot score RILPL2. The eight claims of Figures 1 to 5 were blocked in attempt -01 under pilot-6; under pilot-7 they are tested on the data the paper deposited elsewhere and are counted apart from the dandiset's claims.

A failure to reproduce here may be a failure of this attempt, not of the paper: see the reasoning and the differences from the paper's method.

How the analysis differs from the paper's:

  • The evoked integral is taken over the light-on period, as the Methods state; the paper's numbers come from the code's window, 0.1 s before to 1.0 s after onset (its published integrals equal that measure times 0.0001). Both are shown.
  • Spontaneous transients are measured by their integral, as the Methods state; the paper's published values are 0.005 times the integral divided by the number of samples in each transient. Both are shown; the published measure gives the paper's Figure 6F p-value and per-mouse count exactly.
  • Per-mouse tests are shown under four readings, as the Methods (Welch), the legends (one-tailed) and the code (Student, two-tailed) disagree.
  • The window chunking_index.m computes as written starts 1 s after onset; the source data show the paper used the intended window starting 1 s before onset. The literal window is shown as a variant only.
  • The claims of Figures 1, 2E to 2G, 4I and 5 start from the paper's deposited per-section, per-area and per-blot values, as the Imaris analyses and the blot quantification cannot be repeated here. Figure 2B starts from the deposited peptide abundances without normalisation, which the criterion did not fix; a median-centred variant is shown. Figure 3 uses log2 intensities, where the paper's p-values are on intensities without the log; RILPL2 has no pair for the paired test, so it does not hold under the criterion, and the Methods' imputation is shown as a variant. Figure 4D and 4E add a re-implementation of the Methods' FIJI procedure in Python. One Figure 5 section entered twice is counted once.

What was found about the dandiset:

  • The Anxa1 recordings are those behind Figure 6 and Supplementary Figure 7: the matched published traces equal the dandiset's dF/F to within 5.7e-13, and the evoked integrals and transient counts match, except one stimulation of mouse 4398 that the processed series cuts off 0.8 s after onset.
  • The Calb1 dF/F in the dandiset is not the trace behind Supplementary Figure 8. None of the 384 published traces or integrals match it, no epoch of any power matches a published trace, and recomputing from the raw signal with any single background fraction does not close the gap. The raw signal is there, but the processing the paper used for Calb1 is not, so the Calb1 results here are of the dandiset's processing, not the paper's.
  • The epochs table describes one kind of train and four powers; the files hold two kinds of train and eight powers, and two Anxa1 GS mice received the paper's powers as 0.33 s trains of 9 ms pulses; in these two mice the response does not follow the labelled power.
  • The dF/F unit is given as a.u. for a series in percent; two trains have a pulse length of 0; the four excluded mice are left out without a note; the archive summary lists a behavioral approach; and the paper does not cite the dandiset. The dandiset does not link to the Zenodo, PRIDE and BioImage Archive deposits that hold the rest of the paper's data. None of these findings of attempt -01 is fixed.

What was found about the data in other archives:

  • In PRIDE PXD065006 and Supplementary data 1, the RAB3 T86 phosphopeptide is higher in the samples labelled MLi-2, and the paper's volcano table is MLi-2 minus vehicle (to within 1.6e-06 after a constant), while the legend reads a positive difference as higher with vehicle. The table gives 254 peptides at the legend's thresholds, not 289.
  • The paper's counts of 69 and 16 RAB3A-preferring and p-RAB3A-preferring proteins are at adjusted p < 0.05, where the text says p-value < 0.05; its Figure 1D p-value is not that of the test the legend names.
  • One Figure 5D/5E section appears twice in the source data; counting it once moves one comparison to p = 0.058. Figure 4E has 51 GS areas against the legend's 57, and the 5E legend repeats the 5D genotype F.
  • The source data do not identify the GS animals of Figures 5G, 5H and 5J, and the image studies hold images and mice that the source data do not (an extra WT mouse in the Anxa1 study, mouse 1923 against 1723, more images than sections), without saying which images the figures used. The OME metadata of three synaptosome images of S-BIAD2074 give 488 nm for all three channels.
